Lessons.Title: One- and Two-step Comparison Problems
ExplanationParagraphs:
Learning goal: You will solve multiplicative comparison word problems with one or two steps.
In this lesson, you apply what you learned about interpreting and representing multiplicative comparison situations to problems in context. The numbers you encounter here are larger, encouraging them to transition from discrete diagrams to more-abstract tape diagrams in which each section is labeled to represent a quantity (MP2). You continue to write equations with symbols representing the unknown and to describe the meaning of your equations in the context of the word problems.
Core relationship: One- and two-step comparison problems. Model the multiplicative step first; then perform the required increase, decrease, or combination.

Local publisher 2021 source lesson activities: Warm-up:  Which One Doesn’t Belong: Something's Missing (10 minutes); Activity 1:  The Book Fair	 (20 minutes); Activity 2:  More Book Fair Purchases	 (15 minutes); Cool-down:  Comics and Posters	 (5 minutes)
Source-aligned Edulytics model: A fair sold six groups of eight tickets and four more. Total?
First-party Cool-down (not gated original): A display contains 5 groups of 12 books and 7 extras. Total?
Original visual/physical and peer-explanation activities still require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: One- and two-step comparison problems
KeyConcepts.Rule: Model the multiplicative step first; then perform the required increase, decrease, or combination.
KeyConcepts.Example: A fair sold six groups of eight tickets and four more. Total?

KeyConcepts.Title: Mathematical relationship
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two-step multiplicative problems require checking the relationship at each step.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two-step multiplicative problems require checking the relationship at each step.
KeyConcepts.Example: There are 8 cards. One class has triple and another has double the triple. How many?

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact inverse and unit check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Addition and multiplication express distinct comparisons.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Addition and multiplication express distinct comparisons.
KeyConcepts.Example: A collection has 12 items; another has four times as many, then 7 are removed. How many left?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing a 'times' relation into an addition before the comparison step.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the unit, place value, or operation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Model the multiplicative step first; then perform the required increase, decrease, or combination.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding multipliers in a sequential multiplicative situation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The comparison ratio or measurement units do not match the task.
CommonMistakes.Correction: If a quantity is doubled then tripled, the factor is six.
